title: Begin Each Day with a 10-Minute Stretch Routine, Increasing to 20 Minutes over Time
subtitle: Start a Morning Stretch Routine
description: Begin each day with a 10-minute stretch routine, increasing to 20 minutes over time.

lifeOsSource.hack: Begin each day with a 10-minute stretch routine, increasing to 20 minutes over time.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Use a short, gentle flexibility routine as a morning movement cue if that timing suits you. Move slowly only as far as is comfortable, start with a few simple movements, and build up gradually rather than forcing a fixed 10-to-20-minute progression.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did the movements feel comfortable and controlled? Did I stop or modify anything that caused pain or made me feel unwell, and is this routine still appropriate for me?

faq.question: Does the routine need to last 10 minutes?
faq.answer: No. Ten minutes can be a convenient starting boundary, but there is no universal evidence-based duration for a morning flexibility routine. Start with a small comfortable sequence and build gradually if it remains appropriate.

faq.question: How far should I stretch?
faq.answer: Move slowly only as far as is comfortable and do not force range. The NHS flexibility examples repeatedly use comfort as the boundary and recommend building up gradually.

faq.question: When should I get medical advice before using the routine?
faq.answer: Get advice from a healthcare professional if you are unsure whether the exercises suit your fitness level, or if you have a health problem, injury, symptoms, feel unwell, have had a recent serious health event or operation, or are pregnant or recently gave birth. Stop exercising if you feel pain or become unwell.

intro.html: A short morning flexibility routine can be used as a simple movement cue if mornings suit your schedule. The timing and duration are practical choices, not a medical prescription. The NHS describes gentle flexibility exercises that can be done at home, recommends moving only as far as is comfortable, and advises building up gradually.

sections.title: 1. Choose a small sequence
sections.html: Start with a few gentle movements rather than designing a complete mobility programme. The NHS flexibility guide includes examples such as neck rotation, a sideways bend and a calf stretch. Use established instructions for the movement you choose instead of inventing a more aggressive variation.

sections.title: 2. Use comfort as the boundary
sections.html: Move slowly and only as far as is comfortable. Do not force range to complete a timer, rep count or target position. A shorter comfortable session is preferable to turning a simple routine into a test of tolerance.

sections.title: 3. Treat duration as a setting, not a dose
sections.html: If ten minutes fits your morning, use it as a simple boundary. If a shorter sequence is more appropriate, use that. The NHS notes that there are no specific recommendations for how much time should be spent on strength and flexibility exercises, so Brali does not prescribe a 10-to-20-minute progression as an evidence-based target.

sections.title: 4. Build up gradually
sections.html: When the routine remains comfortable and useful, add a movement, a repetition or a little more time gradually. Do not increase duration simply to maintain a streak or hit a preset progression rule.

sections.title: 5. Use clear safety boundaries
sections.html:
The NHS exercise safety guidance recommends getting healthcare advice before trying general exercises if you are unsure they are suitable for your fitness level, or if you have a health problem, injury, symptoms, feel unwell, have had a recent serious health event or operation, or are pregnant or recently gave birth. Stop the exercise if you feel pain or become unwell.

This Brali entry is general educational material. It is not a treatment plan for pain, injury or a medical condition.

sections.title: 6. Review suitability, not streak length
sections.html: In Brali, record whether the short routine happened, whether the movements felt comfortable and controlled, and whether anything needed to be stopped or modified. The useful signal is whether the routine remains appropriate and easy to perform safely, not whether you reached a prescribed number of minutes.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace an inherited stretching article containing unsupported recovery, pain, heart-rate, adherence, and progression claims with a conservative flexibility routine grounded in current NHS exercise guidance and safety information.
